newsitem.title: UK: Dollar ends lower in Europe on trade/EMU concerns.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends lower in Europe on trade/EMU concerns.

text.p: The dollar ended more than 1-1/2 pfennigs and more than two yen lower in Europe, weighed down by a combination of concerns about European monetary union and U.S. protests at swelling Japanese trade surpluses, traders said.

The mark was lifted after French reservations about the details of the post-EMU budgetary stability pact were expressed at the European Union finance ministers meeting in Luxembourg, adding to jitters about a delay to the 1999 EMU start date.
The yen led the way in early trading, however, pushing the dollar down to a six-month-low about 111.80 and extending the Japanese unit's gains since May 1 to 12.3 percent.
"Dollar/yen was the mover overnight but it's all been dollar/mark and EMU-related trading since then," said Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase Investment Bank.

"The mood surrounding EMU is nervous but there is still an underlying confidence it will go ahead on time," said Schmidt. "What we have realized, however, is that the mark is still being played as the European safe-haven - on the knee-jerk at least."
At 1520 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.7065/75 marks compared with 1.7250/60 late in Europe on Friday. Against the yen, the dollar was at 112.46/56 compared with 115.19/24 late last week.

Dollar/yen sales overnight were a follow-through from late Friday when U.S. Trade respresentative Charlene Barshefsky reiterated recent comments from U.S. Treasury Secreatary Robert Rubin that Japan could not export its way out of recession.

Both warned against the rising Japanese trade surpluses and raised concerns the trade issue, and by extension the level of dollar/yen, would be central to the summit of the Group of Seven industrialised nations in Denver on July 20-22.
"There's going to be a lot of volatility in this rate right up to the G7 meeting later this month," said Peter Wood, trader at Bank of Boston in London.

The EMU story boiled over later in the day after French officials said they would consult their National Assembly before fully endorsing the budget stability. French finance minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said an agreement on the pact had not yet been reached.
However, a raft of other senior EU politicians, including Strauss-Kahn and his German counterpart Theo Waigel, later said they remained confident EMU would start on time in 1999.
Traders said the mark hgad fallen to such low levels in recent weeks that it made sense to buy back some simply for insurance against the outside chance of a delay.

"The initial reaction is to go for marks but an EMU delay in no good for Germany economically and the ultimate beneficiary will most likely be the dollar anyway," said Wood at Bank of Boston, who saw dollar/mark as good value below 1.70.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl today warned those talking of an EMU delay of the effects that would have on the mark and German exports.
A surge of demand for marks on an unravelling of the single currency process would risk making German exports, one of the few bright spots for the German economy at present, less competitive.
The dollar also suffered today from uncertainty about the outcome of the Federal Reserve's policy-making Open Market Committee on Juy 1-2.

Although many economists said the May U.S. employment report from last Friday showed still-strong U.S. growth, the interest rate market has shifted back expectations of a rate rise and the market is now only positioned 50-50 for a move next month.
